Barrie Tenant Heating and AC Rights

Conversation with Gemini

You said

As Tenants in Barrie, Ontario, Canada in a Basement Suite, with the Upstairs unit vacant and secured, what obligations does the landlord have to ensure comfortable temperatures for the tenants?


As it stands, the landlord has manually set the thermostat upstairs to a "comfortable" temperature (71 F / 21.6667 C), and yet the actual temperature downstairs has dipped to 17 C


A AC Unit is also installed in this house and as the summer season approaches, the unit being too hot is also a concern for us.

Gemini said

In Ontario, and specifically within the City of Barrie, landlords are legally required to maintain specific temperature standards to ensure a rental unit is habitable. Since you are currently experiencing temperatures of 17°C, your landlord is likely in violation of both provincial law and local municipal by-laws.

Here is a breakdown of the landlord's obligations and your rights as a tenant.

1. Minimum Heat Requirements

In Barrie, the Adequacy and Maintenance By-law dictates the heating standards for rental properties.

  • The Temperature Standard: Landlords must ensure that every room in a rental unit is maintained at a minimum temperature of 21°C (70°F).

  • The "Heating Season": This requirement is in effect from September 1 to June 15 of the following year.

  • The Current Issue: Since it is currently May and your unit is at 17°C, the landlord is failing to meet the municipal standard, regardless of what the thermostat is set to in the upstairs unit. The law cares about the temperature where you live, not where the sensor is located.

2. Thermostat Access and Vital Services

Under the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), heat is considered a vital service.

  • Exclusive Control: If the landlord has exclusive control over the thermostat (because it is in a locked, vacant unit), they have a heightened responsibility to ensure the settings actually result in legal temperatures in your suite.

  • Interference with Services: By keeping the heat at a level that results in 17°C in your unit, the landlord may be "interfering with a vital service," which is a serious offense under the RTA.

3. Air Conditioning and Summer Heat

Unlike heating, Ontario law does not currently have a province-wide "maximum temperature" or a requirement for landlords to provide air conditioning unless it is specifically mentioned in your lease.

  • If AC is in your Lease: If the lease states AC is provided, the landlord must maintain the unit in good working order. They cannot simply choose not to turn it on if the unit reaches uncomfortable levels.

  • "Reasonable Enjoyment": Even if AC isn't in the lease, the landlord cannot allow the unit to become so hot that it is uninhabitable. However, without a specific maximum heat by-law in Barrie (like the 26°C rule in Toronto), this is harder to enforce than the 21°C heating rule.

Recommended Action Steps

Step 1: Formal Written Notice

Send a polite but firm email or letter to the landlord. Mention the specific temperature you recorded and the date/time.

"The temperature in our suite has dropped to 17°C. Under the Barrie Adequacy and Maintenance By-law, the unit must be maintained at a minimum of 21°C until June 15. Because we do not have access to the thermostat, please adjust the upstairs settings or provide a solution to bring our unit up to the legal minimum immediately."

Step 2: Contact Barrie By-law Enforcement

If the landlord does not rectify the heat within 24–48 hours, contact the City of Barrie Building and By-law Services. They can send an inspector to your home to measure the temperature. If it is below 21°C, they can issue a Work Order or a fine to the landlord to force compliance.

Step 3: File with the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB)

If the issue persists or the landlord refuses to address the AC in the summer (assuming it’s in your lease), you can file a Form T6 (Tenant Application about Maintenance). You may be entitled to a rent abatement (a partial refund) for the time you lived in a unit that did not meet legal standards.

Note: If you find yourself needing to use space heaters to stay warm in the meantime, keep track of any significant increase in your electricity bill. You can claim these costs back through the LTB if the landlord is found to be failing their maintenance obligations.

How long has the temperature been sitting at 17°C, and have you already had any discussions with the landlord about the thermostat placement?
